(a) SOR/2007-303 s. 3.1 (DIVISION 1 definitions) names the framework three times, once for each of three capital-formation aggregates: 'gross fixed capital formation in intellectual property products, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'; 'gross fixed capital formation in machinery and equipment, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'; 'gross fixed capital formation in non-residential structures, as determined by Statistics Canada on the basis of data for or from its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. (b) SOR/2007-303 s. 5(b)(i), the DIVISION 1 all-provinces revenue base: 'the portion of the aggregate of corporate profits in Canada, before the payment of income taxes and without any deduction of the aggregate of corporate losses in Canada, that is attributable to any of the 10 provinces for the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. [evidence: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SOR-2007-303/page-3.html]

(c) Two further terms of the same formula at SOR/2007-303 s. 8(1)(y) are pinned to the national accounts. 'A is the total wages and salaries excluding supplementary labour income, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts, paid in the province in the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, other than the wages and salaries paid by (i) the federal general government sector to employees in the defence industry, and (ii) the provincial and territorial general government sector and the local general government sector to their employees'. And 'M is military pay and allowances, excluding supplementary labour income, paid in the province in the calendar year that ends in the fiscal year, as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. RESOLVED 2026-08-08 (Thomas, Open-Questions-2026-08-08-sweep.docx Q1): the Regulations name the *System of Macroeconomic Accounts* itself, not a specific release, and Thomas's ruling was to mint the framework as its own node rather than infer a mapping to one of its releases. Target repointed from the inferred statcan-national-accounts (IMDB record 1901, GDP by income and expenditure) to statcan-system-macroeconomic-accounts, which now matches the statutory wording verbatim rather than through a judgement call. targetReport.title: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts
targetReport.description: The overarching accounting framework Statistics Canada operates under for macroeconomic statistics -- the umbrella that the quarterly income-and-expenditure accounts (statcan-national-accounts, IMDB record 1901), monthly GDP by industry (statcan-gdp-monthly), the Supply and Use Tables (statcan-sut) and the National Balance Sheet Accounts all sit inside, per the User Guide's own chapter structure and per record 1901's language describing the annual benchmarks as arising 'through the construction of annual supply and use tables' within this system. Minted as a node in its own right 2026-08-08 because two federal fiscal-transfer regulations (SOR/2007-303, both the Equalization and Territorial Formula Financing divisions) name the framework itself -- not a specific release -- as the thing a statutory wage/salary term is 'determined... for the purpose of': 'as determined by Statistics Canada for the purpose of its System of Macroeconomic Accounts'. Thomas's ruling (2026-08-08, Open-Questions-2026-08-08-sweep.docx Q1): frameworks and legislative instruments a regulation is built on are worth a node even with no cadence of their own -- 'its sole role is broadcasting and that needs represented.' No releases_per_year: this is an evergreen framework, not a periodic release, the same shape as the one-off foundational instruments already in the corpus.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

release_schedule.note: ISSAI 300 (Performance Audit Principles) is an INTOSAI/IFPP professional pronouncement, not a periodic statistical release. It was endorsed in 2001, substantially reformulated in 2013, and renamed with editorial changes in 2019 under the IFPP. INTOSAI's Due Process for the IFPP states that revision timing is not centrally fixed: 'The working groups decide on an appropriate frequency at which the regular review shall be carried out,' with maintenance frequency to be communicated per-standard on issai.org. As of the current standard-setting projects list on issai.org/standards-in-setting/, ISSAI 300 is not listed as an active revision project, so there is no known upcoming or scheduled next edition. Revisions have occurred irregularly (2001, 2013, 2019) at the discretion of the responsible performance-audit working group rather than on a fixed calendar.

targetReport.title: Property Assessment Notice and Assessment Roll (Current Value Assessment)
targetReport.description: Ontario's single province-wide property assessment, prepared by a not-for-profit corporation funded by all Ontario municipalities rather than by a government department. This is the structural difference from Alberta, where each municipality prepares its own roll and the province must then run an explicit equalization step to make them comparable. Ontario needs no equalization because there is one assessor. The standard is Current Value, defined in the Assessment Act s. 1(1) as 'the amount of money the fee simple, if unencumbered, would realize if sold at arm's length by a willing seller to a willing buyer'. MPAC states it uses 'one of three approaches to value properties: direct comparison approach, income approach, cost approach', with the direct comparison approach 'the most commonly used' and the choice depending on 'property type, and the number of recent comparable sales of similar properties in the area'. The returned roll and its household counts are what the Ontario Municipal Partnership Fund allocates against.
targetReport.cadence_note: The roll returns annually; the values in it have not been re-based since 2016, and the gap between those two facts is the point. The Assessment Act s. 19.2(1) sets a four-year cycle by schedule, and para 4 assigns 1 January 2016 to 'the four taxation years from 2017 to 2020'. MPAC states the schedule has been suspended: 'On August 16, 2023, the Ontario government filed a regulation to amend the Assessment Act, extending the postponement of a province-wide reassessment through the end of the 2021-2024 assessment cycle. Property assessments for the 2026 property tax year will continue to be based on fully phased-in January 1, 2016 current values.' So `releases_per_year` 1 counts the returned roll, which does move for new construction, demolition and change of use; `changes_per_year` 0.25 is the statutory reassessment cycle, which is the rate at which the valuation basis is supposed to move and has not moved in ten years. Both numbers are true and neither alone describes this node.

release_schedule.note: MPAC delivers an assessment roll annually to Ontario municipalities each Nov-Dec (with Property Assessment Notices mailed to owners with changed assessments in November, and the roll formally 'returned' in early-mid December: Dec 12 2023, Dec 10 2024, ~Dec 9 2025). This annual notice/roll cycle is distinct from the province-wide Current Value Assessment (CVA) base-year update: Ontario's Assessment Act nominally requires reassessment on a 4-year cycle, but the government has repeatedly postponed it by regulation since 2020 (most recently confirmed through the 2026 tax year), so assessed values remain frozen at January 1, 2016 current values with no announced date for the next province-wide reassessment. The annual roll-return/notice cycle, however, has continued on schedule every year regardless of the reassessment freeze.

targetReport.title: Financial Information Return (FIR)
targetReport.publisher: Ontario Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing
targetReport.description: Ontario's mandatory annual municipal financial return — the direct counterpart of `ab-municipalaffairs-fir`, already a node in this graph for Alberta. The FIR portal describes it as 'a standardized reporting of a municipality's financial activities in the previous fiscal year (January to December)', collecting data on assets, liabilities, revenue, expenses and statistical information drawn from each municipality's audited financial statements. Mandatory under the Municipal Act s. 294(1): 'the treasurer of a municipality shall in each year provide the Minister with a return containing information designated by the Minister with respect to the financial affairs of the municipality.' Named directly in the OMPF Technical Guide's Appendix F: 'PIL Weighted Assessment | 2023 or 2024 | Municipal FIR (Financial Information Return)'. Minted 2026-08-09 (corpus-wide `_dropped` sweep, Tier-1 item #7).
targetReport.cadence_note: Annual, deadline 31 May per the FIR portal's own description of the submission cycle; collected since 1978 (covering 1977 financial data), with complete province-wide datasets from 1988 onward per the portal's own historical archive.

release_schedule.rule: The deadline for the completion of the [year] Financial Information Return (FIR) is May 31 of the following year (e.g., "The deadline for the completion of 2025 FIR is May 31, 2026"), per the FIR Instructions issued by the Ontario Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing under Municipal Act s.294(1).
release_schedule.note: The 2025 FIR deadline of May 31, 2026 has already passed as of 2026-08-11; next occurrence is the 2026 FIR, due May 31, 2027, following the same annual pattern. Deadline is stated in the annual FIR Instructions document (page 9, 'Deadline for Completion' section) rather than a fixed statutory date, but has been consistently May 31 in recent years.

This session independently fetched the EAC's own instrument and confirmed it applies to Tanzania by name: 'The East African Community (EAC) is the regional inter-governmental organisation of the Republics of Kenya, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania (URT), Republic of Rwanda, Republic of Burundi and Republic of South Sudan' (Foreword), with Article 2002 stating 'These regulations shall apply to all EAC Partner States for the compilation of Harmonised Consumer Price Indices' and Article 110.1: 'The classification used for the compilation of the HCPI and its sub-indices shall be based on the most recent official United Nations Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP).' targetReport.title: EAC Regulations for Compiling Harmonised Consumer Price Indices (HCPI)
targetReport.description: A binding East African Community instrument (March 2022) requiring Partner States to compile and submit a Harmonised CPI to the EAC Secretariat, for regional comparability and East African Monetary Union convergence-criteria monitoring -- described as binding in its entirety and directly applicable, and classification 'shall be based on the most recent official United Nations Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP)'. Filed `supranational` rather than `international` on the same reasoning the corpus already applies to the EU's ESA 2010: a regional body legislating a binding, directly-applicable obligation, not a standard adopted by choice. Distinct from Kenya's own domestic CPI, which aligns with these regulations' spirit (per KNBS's own rebasing report) without the regulations themselves directly governing the domestic release -- the binding obligation is to also produce the separate HCPI submission.
targetReport.cadence_note: The regulatory instrument itself, not an annual release; nominal cadence matching the treatment given to esa-2010 and other framework-level nodes.

release_schedule.note: This is a one-off legal/regulatory instrument (EAC Regulations for Compiling Harmonised Consumer Price Indices, published March 2022), not a recurring statistical publication. The document itself was 'gazetted' with a target entry-into-force date of 31 Dec 2024 (Article 106), a one-time milestone, not a recurring cycle. Internally it does specify review cycles for the underlying CPI methodology (weights reviewed at max 5-year intervals per Art. 704.1, mini-surveys every 2-3 years per Art. 704.2, EAC-level weights every 3-5 years per Art. 706.5, annual compliance reports per Art. 113.3), but none of these are a stated periodicity for reissuing or amending the Regulations document itself. There is no found evidence of a fixed amendment/republication cadence for the Regulations text, so releases_per_year probably should not be treated as a fixed number for this report at all -- it is better modeled as irregular (amended only when the EAC Council/Secretariat decides to revise it) rather than assigned any specific interval.

results.basis: RE-CITED 2026-09-05 (Round C): the gov.za media statement previously cited never mentions the Constitution (round 5's Section 224 quote came from the Constitution itself). The SARB's own monetary-policy page — the source node's url — states the constitutional mandate in its own words; cited and quoted from there instead. Section 224 of the Constitution: 'The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth in the Republic.' This resolves the open question left in za-fiscal-federalism.json about the SARB's statutory basis: the 3% (±1pp) numerical target itself is NOT written into the South African Reserve Bank Act 90 of 1989 (which only carries the older 'protect the value of the currency' language) -- it was set by a 2025 agreement between the Minister of Finance and the SARB Governor ('The Minister of Finance today announced a new inflation target for South Africa of 3% with a 1 percentage point tolerance band. This decision follows agreement between the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) and the Minister.'). A third South African mechanism, after grants (Gazette notice) and UIF (Gazette notice), that turns out to be discretionary/agreement-based rather than a hard statutory formula.
results.evidenceQuote: The SARB’s mandate, set out in the Constitution, requires it to protect the value of the rand in the interest of balanced and sustainable growth.

targetReport.title: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 — Chapter 13 (Finance)
targetReport.description: The constitutional basis for how revenue is split among South Africa's three spheres of government. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session. s.213: money raised nationally goes into the National Revenue Fund, and 'a province's equitable share of revenue raised nationally' is 'a direct charge against the National Revenue Fund'. s.214(1)(a): 'An Act of Parliament must provide for... the equitable division of revenue raised nationally among the national, provincial and local spheres of government'; s.214(2) lists the factors that Act must weigh, including provinces' and municipalities' ability to 'provide basic services' and 'fiscal capacity and efficiency'. s.226 gives each province its own Revenue Fund; s.227(1)(a) entitles local government and provinces to 'an equitable share of revenue raised nationally... to provide basic services'. ss.228-229 give provinces and municipalities limited own-revenue powers (no income tax, VAT or customs duty for either).
